headline: Sharks may help predict the next hurricane

sources.title: US scientists turn to sharks for help with hurricane prediction (France 24)
Sharks Equipped with Sensors Provide New Clues for Hurricane Forecasting (MARACOOS)
Scientists turn to sharks to improve hurricane predictions (The Japan Times)
Scientists attach sensors to sharks to track hurricanes (video, ABC News)

chunks.text: What does a [[hurricane]] eat? Warm ocean water. Big storms {{feed on}} heat near the sea [[surface]], and a [[patch]] of unusually warm water can {{set off}} rapid growth in a passing storm. To [[predict]] that growth, [[forecasters]] need to know how warm the ocean is, and not just at the top. The problem: the open sea is huge, and much of it is never measured.

verbs.why: Mosquitoes feed on blood, and rumors feed on gossip and fear. Hurricanes feed on warm ocean water near the surface, which fuels their growth.
A spark can set off a fire alarm, and one rumor can set off a panic. In the ocean, a patch of unusually warm water can set off rapid storm growth.

chunks.text: Now scientists in the United States are getting help from an [[unusual]] team. Researchers at the University of Delaware {{went over}} more than 20 years of shark-tracking [[records]], species by species, and {{settled on}} two kinds that often swim near the surface: shortfin mako sharks and blue sharks. Small [[sensors]] on their [[fins]] measure the temperature, [[depth]], and [[saltiness]] of the water. Whenever a shark {{comes up}} to the surface, the tags {{send back}} the [[measurements]] to scientists on [[shore]] by [[satellite]].

verbs.why: Lawyers go over contracts line by line, and students go over notes before a test. The Delaware team went over twenty years of shark tracking records before choosing which species to use.
Couples settle on a wedding date, and friends settle on a restaurant after arguing for an hour. After reviewing the data, scientists settled on mako and blue sharks for the project.

verbs.correct: To return information to a place
verbs.why: Weather satellites send back photos of storms, and space robots send back pictures from far away. Here a shark's tag sends back ocean measurements to scientists on shore by satellite.

verbs.correct: To rise to a higher place
verbs.why: Divers come up for air, and swimmers come up between strokes. These sharks come up to the surface about twice a day, giving their tags a chance to transmit.

chunks.text: Why sharks? Machines have limits. A research [[robot]] can {{break down}}, and a weather [[buoy]] stays in one place. Sharks never stop swimming, and they travel [[up and down]] through the water all day, taking the sensors with them. Makos {{turned out}} to be a [[perfect fit]], because they visit the surface about twice a day, which gives the tags a [[chance]] to send their data home.

verbs.wrong: To become too hot to touch
verbs.why: Cars break down on the highway, and old machines break down without warning. Unlike a shark, an underwater robot can break down and simply stop working at sea.
A rumor can turn out false, and a plan can turn out better than expected. Mako sharks turned out to be an excellent choice, since they visit the surface so often.

chunks.text: The project is {{starting out}} small, with only a [[handful]] of tagged sharks so far, and the [[engineers]] are still [[improving]] the tags. But every measurement counts. More tagged sharks could {{fill in}} the empty spots on the ocean map, in waters that storms pass [[on their way to]] land. Better maps of ocean heat mean better [[forecasts]], and better forecasts give [[coastal]] towns more time to prepare or {{get out}} before a storm arrives.

verbs.correct: To begin in a small way
verbs.wrong: To fail at an early stage
verbs.why: A small business can start out in a garage, and a hike can start out on flat ground. This shark project is starting out small, with only a handful of tagged animals so far.
People fill in a form at the doctor's office, and reporters fill in missing details in a story. More tagged sharks could fill in the empty spots on the map of ocean heat.

verbs.wrong: To hide in a safe building
verbs.why: Families get out of a burning house fast, and drivers get out of a flooded car. Better hurricane forecasts give coastal towns more time to prepare or get out safely.

mainIdea.s: Scientists are putting small sensors on sharks to measure heat inside the ocean. The data returns by satellite and could make hurricane forecasts much better.
mainIdea.why: Tagged makos and blue sharks carry sensors that send back temperature, depth, and saltiness data that forecasters need.

mainIdea.s: Sharks with sensors already guide every single hurricane warning in the United States. Thanks to the animals, forecasters predicted each storm this summer perfectly.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the project is just starting out, with only a handful of tagged sharks. It may improve forecasts in the future.

mainIdea.s: Scientists trained a group of sharks to swim away from hurricanes and lead fish to safer water. The animals learned to feel a storm coming days before it arrived.
mainIdea.why: The article is about sharks carrying sensors that measure the ocean, not about sharks protecting fish from storms.
